articles.title: Espanha pede suspensão do TikTok após denúncias de abuso infantil | G1
articles.standfirst: Investigação identificou 1.183 publicações explícitas na plataforma, com pelo menos 48 milhões de visualizações; governo acionou Ministério Público e órgão de proteção de dados.
articles.summary: Investigação identificou 1.183 publicações explícitas na plataforma, com pelo menos 48 milhões de visualizações; governo acionou Ministério Público e órgão de proteção de dados.
articles.body:
O governo da Espanha pediu que o TikTok suspenda suas operações no país até que a plataforma elimine conteúdos de abuso sexual infantil.

A solicitação foi feita nesta terça-feira (10), após uma investigação identificar 1.183 publicações explícitas desse tipo na rede social, que somaram milhões de visualizações.

A ministra da Juventude da Espanha, Sira Rego, encaminhou o pedido ao Ministério Público e à Agência de Proteção de Dados do país. A pasta não tem autoridade para determinar, sozinha, a suspensão da plataforma.

"Redes sociais não podem ser territórios sem lei", afirmou Rego, em comunicado.

O pedido ocorre meses depois de o governo espanhol solicitar uma investigação sobre X, Meta e TikTok por suspeita de disseminação de material de abuso sexual infantil gerado por inteligência artificial (IA).

O caso acontece em meio ao aumento da fiscalização de empresas de tecnologia por reguladores europeus, que têm ampliado a pressão sobre as plataformas para combater conteúdos ilegais e prejudiciais.

Investigação identificou milhões de visualizações

Uma investigação publicada na segunda-feira (9) pela organização espanhola de checagem de fatos Maldita.es identificou 1.183 publicações explícitas de abuso sexual infantil no TikTok.

Segundo a entidade, os vídeos foram visualizados pelo menos 48 milhões de vezes. Mais de 26 mil perfis comentaram ou compartilharam o material.

Em uma atualização publicada na noite de terça-feira, a organização informou que o TikTok restringiu duas expressões usadas nas buscas que levavam a esse tipo de conteúdo para usuários na Espanha.

Apesar da medida, pesquisas feitas em outros países europeus ainda direcionavam os usuários às mesmas publicações.

Procurado pela Reuters, o TikTok não respondeu imediatamente ao pedido de comentário.

articles.title: Papa pede que Milei supere tensões com Lula em referência indireta | G1
articles.standfirst: Mensagem procurou incentivar o diálogo para superar graves tensões num momento em que o presidente argentino ofende líderes da região, principalmente Lula, deixando as históricas relações bilaterais à beira da ruptura.
articles.summary: Em visita à Argentina, o Papa defendeu o diálogo para superar a crise entre Milei e Lula, que levou ao rebaixamento das relações diplomáticas entre os dois países.
articles.body:
O Papa Leão XIII discursa para autoridades, membros da sociedade civil e do corpo diplomático, ao lado do presidente argentino Javier Milei — Foto: REUTERS/Yara Nardi

Foi uma mensagem diplomática, nas entrelinhas, que passou quase despercebida, mas que vários diplomatas captaram com a sensibilidade da linguagem característica.

Logo no seu primeiro discurso durante sua viagem à Argentina , ao lado do presidente Javier Milei , o Papa Leão XIV fez uma intervenção veemente e equilibrada de forte teor político na qual defendeu o diálogo, o respeito e a procura perseverante de acordos para superar graves tensões numa referência indireta às atuais relações diplomáticas da Argentina com o Brasil , mais especificamente entre Milei e Lula .

“Os legítimos interesses de cada nação devem ser defendidos por meio do diálogo, do respeito pelo direito e da procura perseverante de acordos. A América do Sul soube encontrar, nos momentos difíceis da sua história, caminhos de negociação e de entendimento para superar graves tensões”, indicou o Papa, num trecho do seu discurso de 25 minutos, para logo pedir:

“A Argentina é chamada a preservar essa vontade de diálogo e a contribuir para que continue a dar frutos”, apontou Leão XIV num momento em que as relações diplomáticas entre Argentina e Brasil , eixo da integração regional, foram rebaixadas ao passo prévio à ruptura, com a retirada dos embaixadores no dia 4 de agosto passado.

Esse foi o segundo momento do discurso no qual o papa menciona a América do Sul como o espaço no qual a Argentina está inserida com laços indissolúveis com os seus vizinhos.

“Os grandes rios unem territórios; os ecossistemas vão de um país a outro; a energia, os alimentos, o conhecimento e a mobilidade humana criam laços que ultrapassam fronteiras. Por isso, pensar no futuro da Argentina leva-nos também a olhar para os povos com os quais ela compartilha este continente. A América do Sul possui uma enorme riqueza humana e natural, e os seus povos mantêm laços históricos e tradições culturais que proporcionam um amplo campo de cooperação”, descreveu Leão XIV na sua mensagem perante políticos e diplomatas.

Monsenhor Jorge Lozano, arcebispo de San Juan e presidente da comissão episcopal de comunicação social confirmou à RFI que o papa também aludia à tensão diplomática entre Brasil e Argentina como um ponto que deve ser superado.

“Não há um governo que tenha o direito de cortar com décadas de comunhão e de participação bilateral. Pode haver mais afinidade de um governo com outro, mas a falta de afinidade ideológica não pode ir contra de uma trajetória de construção comunitária dos nossos povos”, sublinhou o arcebispo, um dos responsáveis pela comunicação da visita papal.

As boas relações com os países vizinhos foram evocadas por Leão XIV numa chamada de atenção a Milei para o nível de rebaixamento diplomático das atuais relações da Argentina com o Brasil .

“Esta é uma contribuição da vida da Igreja aos nossos povos. Na constituição do Conselho Episcopal Latino-americano e do Caribe, a experiência de caminhar juntos como Igreja na região é uma experiência muito forte”, explicou Jorge Lozano à RFI.

No passado dia 26 de julho, o embaixador brasileiro em Buenos Aires, Júlio Bitelli, foi chamado para consultas a Brasília , depois que, no dia anterior, o presidente argentino, Javier Milei, insultasse o presidente Lula, chamando-o de “ladrão”, de “corrupto” e de “presidiário” , durante o lançamento da candidatura presidencial de Flávio Bolsonaro em São Paulo.

Não há precedentes de um presidente atacar outro no território do vizinho.

Milei proferiu os insultos ao lado do ministro das Relações Exteriores da Argentina , o chanceler Pablo Quirno, quem aplaudiu e incentivou cada palavra de Milei.

Em 4 de agosto, depois de Milei ter repetido as agressões contra o presidente Lula , o chanceler Mauro Vieira reduziu o nível da relação diplomática com a Argentina , mantendo o embaixador Bitelli em Brasília e deixando a Embaixada do Brasil em Buenos Aires ao nível de encarregado de negócios. O mesmo aconteceu do lado argentino em Brasília.

Segundo declarações posteriores do ministro brasileiro das Relações Exteriores, Mauro Vieira , o Brasil esperava um sinal do governo argentino para desandar o conflito diplomático. Porém, passados 15 dias das eleições no Brasil , que consagraram a reeleição do presidente Lula , Javier Milei continua sem nem mesmo cumprimentar o seu par brasileiro pela vitória.

Antecedentes de intervenção do papa em conflito

A maior intervenção de um papa num conflito bilateral envolvendo a Argentina aconteceu em dezembro de 1978. Diferentemente de um conflito meramente diplomático, o Papa João Paulo II evitou uma guerra iminente entre a Argentina e o Chile pela soberania das ilhas Picton, Nueva e Lennox, no Canal de Beagle, na margem Sul da Terra do Fogo.

No Vaticano, João Paulo II convocou os embaixadores e ofereceu a mediação da Santa Sé, enviando urgentemente o cardeal Antonio Samoré a Buenos Aires. A aceitação da proposta, no último minuto, interrompeu a mobilização bélica, quando as tropas já estavam prontas para atacar.

Após anos de negociações discretas, em novembro de 1984, foi assinado o Tratado de Paz e Amizade no Vaticano, posteriormente ratificado por meio de uma consulta popular na Argentina .

Em abril de 1987, já com a Democracia restaurada na Argentina , João Paulo II visitou a Argentina , sendo a última vez que um Papa visitou o país. Foram necessários mais de 39 anos para uma nova visita, a atual do Papa Leão XIV que também tem como objetivo completar a viagem pendente do seu antecessor, o Papa Francisco, quem não retornou à sua terra natal durante os 12 anos do seu papado.

A programação também contará com cinco workshops simultâneos e estandes de exposição, além da entrega do Prêmio Treinar de Empreendedorismo e Gestão Empresarial, às 19h30.

A expectativa é participação de 500 participantes, segundo a organização.

articles.title: Clinton's 'old habit', 'arrogant' Sarkozy & 'real star' Diana: Sonia's candid accounts of world leaders
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Former Congress president Sonia Gandhi recalls in her memoir how then-US president Bill Clinton, during his 2000 India visit, would
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Former Congress president Sonia Gandhi recalls in her memoir how then-US president Bill Clinton, during his 2000 India visit, would occasionally be seen "surreptitiously sizing up the more striking women" at a reception hosted in his honour. The Monica Lewinsky scandal may have faded from the headlines by then, but, as Sonia writes, "old habits die hard".The anecdote is among several candid recollections of Sonia's interactions with global leaders and prominent personalities, including former French president Nicolas Sarkozy and the late Princess Diana, in her newly released memoir, Belonging: A Journey Of Love.Recalling Clinton's 2000 visit, Sonia writes about meeting the then US president at the Sheraton hotel, where he was staying with his daughter Chelsea and his delegation. She had called on him along with then-foreign minister."Friendly, informal, and exuding confidence, he appeared more keen to give us his own views and predictions about Kashmir- 'a nuclear flashpoint', in his words, 'one of the most dangerous places on earth'--than to pay attention to our point of view," she writes.Sonia also recounts a reception hosted by then-prime minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee in Clinton's honour, where she noticed the former US president occasionally looking at women in attendance."The Monica Lewinsky scandal had subsided a little by then, but old habits die hard; at the reception held by Prime Minister Vajpayee in his honour, I noticed him every now and then surreptitiously sizing up the more striking women present," she writes.Sarkozy's love life and an amused SoniaSonia also shares an interesting account of Nicolas Sarkozy's 2008 visit to India, when the French president travelled without his then partner, Carla Bruni."It was said that he (Sarkozy) had been advised not to bring her (Bruni) because they were unmarried which would have been awkward at official functions," she writes.At a banquet, the wife of then vice-president Mohammad Ansari, seated next to Sarkozy, began asking him about his relationship with Bruni, including whether he planned to marry her and whether a date had been fixed."President Sarkozy seemed unperturbed by the cross-examination, even eager to share details of his love life, answering all her questions while continuously messaging his Carla on his phone," Sonia recalls.The couple made a joint appearance in India on a subsequent visit, attending a private dinner hosted by then prime minister Manmohan Singh and his wife.By then, Sarkozy and Bruni had married. Sonia remembers the French president as being visibly besotted with his wife, who had been a popular singer and songwriter in Europe as well as a top model."All eyes were on her as she glided into the room in an elegant long gown, graceful and slim, demure and blue-eyed," she writes.However, Sonia's impression of the evening was not limited to Bruni's appearance. She also recalls Sarkozy holding forth on India's responsibilities while speaking to Manmohan Singh."He was obviously besotted with his tall and beautiful wife of Italian and French descent, who had been a popular singer and songwriter in Europe, as well as a top model. All eyes were on her as she glided into the room in an elegant long gown, graceful and slim, demure and blue-eyed," she writes."She spoke cordially but infrequently--while her husband held forth, expounding his views to our prime minister on what India should do in what I felt was a rather arrogant manner, unmindful of the fact that he was talking to someone more senior, more experienced and more knowledgeable," she adds.Sonia's memories of Princess DianaAmong the most personal recollections in the memoir are Sonia's encounters with the British royal family, particularly Princess Diana.She writes that members of the British royal family had shared a friendship with the Nehru-Gandhi family over generations, while Rajiv Gandhi had got along well with Prince Charles."The real star of that family had of course been Princess Diana: Tall and slim, with large blue eyes, an enchanting smile, and a magnetic personality. I can never forget how ravishing she was as a bride when Rajiv and I attended their wedding in 1981. But when they came to India in 1992, it was evident that things were not going well in the marriage," Sonia writes.She recalls an informal meeting with the royal couple during their 1992 India visit, on the same day Diana famously posed alone on a bench in front of the Taj Mahal, later popularly known as the 'love bench'."On the very day she famously posed alone on what I call the 'love bench' in front of the Taj Mahal, they had come over for a late tea. Prince Charles was forthcoming and amusing, but she appeared morose, though looking wonderful in a striking red and purple two-piece suit. We chatted about what she had seen and liked on her visit," she writes.Sonia's mother, who was visiting at the time, was keen to meet the princess. Her daughter Priyanka was equally eager to introduce her 'Nonna' (grandmother) to Diana.When Diana wondered why Sonia's mother was so quiet, Priyanka immediately explained that she had been told not to speak because she only knew Italian."Diana burst out laughing and turned immediately to my mother, holding out her hand, "Piacere, comne stai?" ("Pleased to meet you, how are you?"), trying to pronounce the words in the correct Italian accent, though using the informal form of address, but with such warmth and charm that we all melted," Sonia recalls.The meeting ended on another warm note. As the royal couple were leaving, Diana stopped midway, turned around and waved to Sonia's mother."After tea and more chat, we were seeing them off to their car when she stopped halfway, turned back to wave to my mother, and called out, 'Ciao. Nonna!' After I presented the royal couple with my book Rajiv, she wrote to me, telling me how much she had admired my husband," Sonia writes.'I am feeling like a crow': An awkward note at the hairdresser'sSonia also recounts a later meeting with Diana in London, when she was invited for tea with the royal couple. She remembers arriving in a black suit with a white collar and joking, "I am feeling like a crow!"On another occasion, she unexpectedly came across Diana at a hairdresser's. Recognising the princess sitting next to her, Sonia decided to pass her a discreet note."I scribbled a word and passed it on to her, and the next second realised that instead of 'Hi', I had written 'Hye'. How I wished I could have snatched back the note! But it was too late; she had already put it into her handbag," she recalls.The two exchanged a few words in hushed tones, careful not to attract attention. It was the last time Sonia met Diana.Reflecting on the public scrutiny surrounding the late princess, Sonia says Diana faced considerable criticism during her lifetime, with many questioning why she appeared unhappy despite her privileged position."There was a lot of criticism of her at that time: She was spoilt and complaining; she had everything; why was she behaving as if she had been wronged? I must say I felt for her throughout, and still do," Sonia writes.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: An Indiana couple paid $100,000 toward a $211,235 modular home but withheld the balance after citing construction problems; a November 9 appeals court upheld a judgment exceeding $221,000 against them
articles.summary: An Indiana couple who paid $100,000 towards a $211,235 modular home but withheld the remaining amount over alleged construction problems have lost their
articles.body: An Indiana couple who paid $100,000 towards a $211,235 modular home but withheld the remaining amount over alleged construction problems have lost their appeal. The Indiana Court of Appeals on November 9 upheld a judgment requiring Tim and Judy McAfee to pay Goeglein Homes, LLC, a total of $221,704.According to the judgment document, the dispute began after the couple hired the company to install a modular home on their property. They raised concerns about the foundation, sloping floors and water entering the crawl space. They argued that the builder had not completed the work as agreed and should not demand the remaining payment.However, the builder maintained that it had substantially fulfilled its contractual responsibilities. It filed a breach-of-contract case after the couple refused to pay the outstanding amount.Couple withheld payment after home inspectionTim and Judy McAfee signed an agreement with Goeglein Homes in December 2021. The original price was $210,650, which increased to $211,235 after they selected a different stove.The company was responsible for preparing the foundation, obtaining permits and completing plumbing work. The couple had to arrange other tasks, including landscaping, electrical service, the driveway, well and septic system.The builder purchased the modular home from Cavco Manufacturing, LLC, and arranged its installation in October 2022. The couple paid $100,000 in December that year, leaving $110,235 outstanding.A home inspection in March 2023 identified concerns including sloping floors, cracked concrete supports, attic framing problems and water entering the crawl space.The disagreement escalated after the builder's project manager visited the property. Judy told him to leave, while Tim later acknowledged that he would not allow the company's employees to return.Goeglein Homes sued the couple in May 2023, claiming they had breached the agreement by withholding payment. The couple filed a counterclaim alleging unresolved construction defects.Court accepts engineer's assessmentThe parties attempted mediation in May 2024 and agreed to complete certain pending work. However, disagreements over the drain tile inspection prevented the settlement from proceeding.During the trial in February 2026, structural engineer Jeremy Bowers examined the property. He concluded that the house met accepted residential construction standards for a modular home.He attributed the foundation cracks to temperature-related shrinkage and said the water accumulation was linked to a downspout issue that fell under the couple's responsibility.The court also considered testimony from Andre Mourad, who was disqualified from giving expert evidence. When asked about the scientific principles behind his findings, Mourad replied, "Quite simply, there are none."The trial court found the builder had substantially performed its contractual obligations by March 20, 2023. It ruled that the couple had breached the agreement by refusing to pay.Appeals court upholds $221,704 judgmentIn April 2026, the trial court ordered the couple to pay $110,235 in outstanding contract payments, along with attorney and expert witness fees. After deducting $8,800 for unfinished work, the judgment stood at $197,889. A subsequent order increased the total to $221,704.The couple challenged the ruling, arguing that the builder had demanded payment before completing its responsibilities and had stopped work on its own.The appeals court rejected their arguments. It noted that the couple had not specifically challenged the finding that the builder had substantially performed its obligations.It also observed that the couple's refusal to allow the company's employees back had prevented the remaining work from being completed. The contract did not require the builder to issue a formal completion notice or written demand for payment.The Indiana Court of Appeals therefore found no reason to overturn the trial court's decision and affirmed the judgment in favour of Goeglein Homes on November 9.You use AI every day. articles.title: A Washington woman paid for a family friend's first home in 2018 and took shared title to secure a $132,000 loan; after he stopped paying, a court upheld his ownership while rejecting his claims against her
articles.summary: A private deal to help a family friend buy his first home led to years of legal battles after loan payments stopped.
articles.body: A private deal to help a family friend buy his first home led to years of legal battles after loan payments stopped. The dispute eventually reached state judges, who had to decide how the property should be owned and how the remaining debt should be handled. The legal dispute began with a 2018 deal between Lorrie D. Carlson and Sonny H. Hwang in Washington state. According to court records from the Court of Appeals of the State of Washington, Division One, Carlson lent Hwang $132,000 to help him buy his first home. As security for the loan, Carlson took a shared ownership interest in the property. The two also signed a promissory note that set out the repayment terms. Under the agreement, Hwang was expected to make monthly payments to reduce the debt. Once the full amount had been repaid, Carlson agreed to sign a quitclaim deed transferring her entire ownership interest in the property to Hwang. However, the arrangement eventually fell apart when Hwang failed to repay the loan. Official court records show that he missed his scheduled payments and later stopped paying altogether. The missed payments led to legal action in state court. Hwang filed claims against Carlson under state law, arguing that her decision to take an ownership interest in the home as security for the loan violated consumer protection laws.Trial court rulings and regulatory claimsThe first court ruling went against Carlson on the legal claims. The trial court found that she had violated Washington's Consumer Loan Act (CLA) and, as a result, the Consumer Protection Act (CPA). The court based its decision on Carlson taking an ownership interest in Hwang's main home as security for the $132,000 loan. The trial court also used its legal powers in the property division case to give Hwang clear ownership of the home. This process is known as quieting title. The court decided that Carlson's financial interest in the property would be protected until Hwang repaid the remaining debt under the promissory note. Carlson appealed the decision. She challenged both the finding that she had broken consumer lending laws and the decision to give Hwang clear title to the property. The appeal was heard by Division One of the Court of Appeals of the State of Washington under case number 87473-0-I.Appellate court rejects consumer law claimsWriting for the appeals court panel, Judge Feldman reviewed the requirements of Washington state law. The judge overturned the lower court's findings that Carlson had violated the consumer protection laws. The appeals court explained that the Consumer Loan Act requires a specific finding before a lender can be held responsible for this type of violation. The lender must either have accepted an ownership interest from the borrower or persuaded the borrower to transfer that interest. In this case, the trial court had not found that Carlson persuaded Hwang to transfer an ownership interest or accepted that interest from him in a way that broke the law. The appeals court therefore ruled that the facts established by the lower court were not enough to prove a violation of the Consumer Loan Act."Where, as here, the plain language of the statute is clear, we must give effect to that plain meaning and 'our inquiry is over,'" Judge Feldman wrote in the opinion. The judge cited established state legal decisions on how courts should interpret laws. The court also rejected the Consumer Protection Act claim. This claim depended entirely on proving that Carlson had violated the Consumer Loan Act. Since the appeals court found no such violation, the Consumer Protection Act claim also failed.Equity title preserved alongside fee recoveryAlthough Carlson succeeded in overturning the findings that she had broken consumer protection laws, the Court of Appeals upheld the trial court's decision to give Hwang clear title to the home. The appeals court explained that trial judges have the power to make fair decisions in property division cases based on the facts of each dispute. The panel agreed that it was reasonable to remove Carlson's ownership interest once Hwang had fully repaid the loan. It found that the trial court had properly used its legal discretion when making this decision.The court also considered the financial responsibilities that resulted from Hwang's missed payments. The promissory note he signed clearly stated that if the loan was sent to an attorney for collection after a default, he would have to pay all collection expenses, including attorney fees. "It is undisputed that Hwang missed and eventually ceased making payments that were due and owing under the Note," the court noted. Since there was no dispute that Hwang had failed to make the required payments, the Court of Appeals ruled that Carlson was entitled to recover the attorney fees she had spent enforcing the promissory note. The case was sent back to the lower court for further proceedings in line with the appeals court's decision.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: At 77, John Glenn made history twice: first orbiting Earth in 1962, then becoming the oldest person in space on Discovery’s 1998 mission
articles.summary: Explore the remarkable journey of John Glenn, who made history as the first American to orbit Earth in 1962 and returned to space at age 77 on the STS-95 mission, contributing to aging research in microgravity.
articles.body: Space exploration has often been associated with young pilots and astronauts trained to handle the physical demands of spacecraft. John Glenn challenged that image when he returned to orbit at the age of 77, more than three decades after his first historic journey. The American astronaut had already made history in 1962 by becoming the first American to orbit the Earth. His second flight aboard the Space Shuttle Discovery in 1998 made him the oldest person to fly in space at the time and brought attention to how ageing affects the human body in space.John Glenn became the first American to orbit Earth in 1962Glenn launched from Cape Canaveral, Florida, aboard the Friendship 7 spacecraft as part of NASA’s Mercury-Atlas 6 mission, NASA.gov reported. He was one of the original seven Mercury astronauts selected by NASA in 1959. His mission aimed to demonstrate that an American astronaut could successfully travel around Earth and return safely. Glenn completed three orbits during the flight, which lasted 4 hours, 55 minutes and 23 seconds. He travelled at approximately 17,500 miles per hour before Friendship 7 splashed down in the Atlantic Ocean. The spacecraft was recovered by the USS Noa, which brought Glenn safely aboard.NASA’s retrospective 60 Years Ago: John Glenn, the First American to Orbit the Earth aboard Friendship 7, describes the mission and its importance during the Space Race between the United States and the Soviet Union. Glenn’s successful flight established the United States as a serious competitor in human orbital spacecraft.Discovery carried Glenn back into space at the age of 77Glenn’s second flight came on October 29, 1998, when he joined the crew of space shuttle Discovery for the STS-95 mission. At 77, he became the oldest person to orbit Earth, a mark nobody has beaten in orbit. Blue Origin’s short suborbital flights later carried William Shatner in 2021 and Ed Dwight in 2024 into space at age 90. Unlike his first mission, Glenn did not command the spacecraft. He served as a payload specialist alongside six other crew members. The mission lasted 8 days, 21 hours and 44 minutes, ending with a landing at Kennedy Space Center on November 7, 1998, NASA’s STS-95 mission page says.NASA’s 25 Years Ago: STS-95, John Glenn Returns to Space records that the mission included more than 80 experiments. These covered several areas of scientific research, including the effects of microgravity on the human body. The paper noted that the seven-member crew completed the work across the shuttle’s middeck, Spacehab and payload bay, including tests on Glenn himself to compare weightlessness with ageing. It also recorded that the flight's 80-plus experiments produced 2,500 Earth observation images and included the four-day SPARTAN free-flyer mission, which the crew deployed and later retrieved.Glenn’s second mission helped scientists study aging in spaceOne of the main reasons for including Glenn in the STS-95 crew was his age. Scientists wanted to investigate whether some physical changes experienced during space resembled those associated with ageing on Earth, the NASA STS-95 mission record explained. During the mission, researchers studied his balance, perception, immune response, bone and muscle density, metabolism, blood flow and sleep patterns. Pedro Duque, another crew member, also participated in some of the medical investigations. Comparing their responses helped researchers examine how age might influence the body's reaction to microgravity. The mission also carried out other scientific activities, including deploying the Spartan satellite to study the Sun and its solar wind.Glenn’s two spaceflights became part of American space historyJohn Glenn’s return to space demonstrated that an astronaut could participate in a major scientific mission well beyond the age usually associated with active spaceflight. His first journey helped establish America’s position in orbital exploration, while his second allowed scientists to study aging in a microgravity environment. Glenn later continued his public service and remained associated with space exploration until his death on December 8, 2016, at the age of 95. His two missions, separated by more than 36 years, remain an unusual chapter in the history of human spaceflight.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: When her husband died of Covid, an Omaha mother of 10 was told his $350,000 life insurance would not pay out; she took the insurer to court twice, and a jury has now awarded her family $11.3 million
articles.summary: A Douglas County jury in Nebraska has awarded $11.3 million (£8.7 million) in damages to an Omaha mother of 10 children.
articles.body: A Douglas County jury in Nebraska has awarded $11.3 million (£8.7 million) in damages to an Omaha mother of 10 children. The jury found that Farmers New World Life Insurance acted in bad faith when it refused to pay her late husband's $350,000 life insurance policy after he died from COVID-19. The verdict was delivered on 16 October 2026, bringing years of legal battles between Vaneza Ramos and the insurance company to a major decision. The details come from court documents and statements released by her lawyers at Pesek Law. The case involved two separate jury trials in the District Court of Douglas County under case number CI 22-2057. The final ruling against the insurer followed a six-year legal fight. It began after Ramos lost her husband and was left to care for her family and newborn baby while facing an uncertain financial future.Policy purchase and claim refusalIn 2018, Ramos's husband, Jose Gaitan, was encouraged by a local Farmers Insurance agent to transfer his existing life insurance coverage to the company. Gaitan then bought a $350,000 (£269,000) life insurance policy. The policy was meant to replace his income if he died. He paid monthly premiums of about $800 (£615). The couple ran a family business in Omaha while raising a blended family of 10 children. In May 2020, the family welcomed their youngest child. Later that month, Gaitan contracted COVID-19 and was admitted to hospital. He died on 31 May 2020. While grieving her husband and caring for her newborn baby, Ramos filed a claim to receive the $350,000 insurance payout. In September 2020, Farmers New World Life Insurance officially rejected her claim. The company pointed to answers about Gaitan's medical history that had been recorded on the original insurance application. Instead of paying the $350,000 death benefit, the insurer offered to return about $17,000 (£13,000) in premiums that had already been paid.Legal challenge over agent conductRamos refused the offer and decided to take the insurance company to court. She hired attorneys Ross Pesek and Alejandra Ayotitla of Pesek Law to represent her family. During the legal case, her lawyers questioned how the insurance agent had completed the original application in 2018. Evidence presented during the trial showed that incorrect answers had been entered about Gaitan's medical history. Text messages also showed that the agent had been told about an earlier hospital stay involving Gaitan's heart before the policy was issued. The legal battle lasted several years and required two separate jury trials to settle different parts of the dispute. The first trial focused on the insurance company's responsibility under the policy contract. The second trial, held in October 2026, dealt with a different question. The jury had to decide whether Farmers Insurance had acted in bad faith and what harm its actions had caused Ramos and her children beyond the unpaid insurance amount. "It's not based on the contract. It's based on the harm," Pesek explained during his closing argument to the jury, according to a press statement published by the National Law Review.Strain on family lifeThe sudden loss of income and the refusal to pay the life insurance benefits placed a heavy burden on the family, according to information released by Pesek Law. To help keep the household running, Ramos's mother moved into the family home to help care for the children. One of Ramos's sons also put his own career plans on hold so he could take on major responsibilities in the family business. Farmers Insurance challenged the amount of financial and emotional harm claimed by the family during the trial. The company argued against the large amount of compensation Ramos and her children were seeking. During his closing argument, Pesek spoke to the jury about the difference between an ordinary person and a large company. He compared the case to the biblical story of David and Goliath. "A promise to protect should not be broken," Pesek told the court. "There is one moment that even Goliath fears. It's this moment. It's accountability because of a jury." He also said that his client had shown great strength throughout the six-year legal battle. "Takes faith. Takes faith for Miss Ramos to think that maybe someday there'll be justice in our community and our world. That if she just holds the line, maybe someday the table will turn. It'll be up to you to decide if that day is today," he said.Jury delivers multi-million awardAfter considering the evidence, the Douglas County jury returned its verdict. It found Farmers New World Life Insurance responsible for acting in bad faith and ordered the company to pay Ramos and her children a total of $11.3 million in damages. The $11.3 million award is meant to cover the harm caused by the insurer's bad-faith actions, rather than simply the original $350,000 value of the life insurance policy. The verdict marks one of the largest bad-faith insurance awards in recent Nebraska history. Farmers Insurance has not publicly confirmed whether it plans to appeal the Douglas County jury's decision.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Paul McCartney, 84, and Ringo Starr, 86, are booked for the same Las Vegas veterans concert on January 29, 2027, setting up a rare reunion of the surviving Beatles more than two years after they last performed together
articles.summary: Paul McCartney and Ringo Starr are set to share the stage once again after being announced as joint headliners for a major charity concert in Las Vegas
articles.body: Paul McCartney and Ringo Starr are set to share the stage once again after being announced as joint headliners for a major charity concert in Las Vegas early next year. The two surviving members of The Beatles, aged 84 and 86 respectively, will reunite on 29 January 2027 at the MGM Grand Garden Arena, according to Rolling Stone. The event will mark their first joint public performance in more than two years. Their last surprise appearance together took place during the final show of McCartney's Got Back tour in London in late 2024. The one-night concert will celebrate the 10th anniversary of VetsAid, an annual charity event started by Eagles guitarist Joe Walsh. The concert raises money for military veterans and their families.Star lineup set for anniversary showOrganisers have announced that the upcoming concert in Nevada will bring together several well-known rock and indie music acts alongside the two former Beatles. Joining McCartney, Starr, and host Joe Walsh will be Las Vegas rock band The Killers, indie rock group The War on Drugs, Grammy-winning singer-songwriter St. Vincent, and indie pop band Lucius. These acts were listed in event details published by music news outlet Consequence. Moving the event to Nevada also means VetsAid will be held in Las Vegas for the first time. Walsh, 78, has spent a lot of time in the city over the past two years while the Eagles have been performing an extended concert residency at the Sphere."Having spent the past two years at the Sphere and working with the hardworking people of Las Vegas, I want to show them my gratitude and respect," Walsh said in an official statement announcing the event."This city has taken such good care of me and my family that it would be my privilege to give back to the large veteran community here and to their families. The VetsAid rock and roll circus is pulling into the MGM Grand Garden and for our tenth anniversary we have our biggest show ever!"Benefit proceeds directed to veteran supportWalsh founded the annual benefit concert in 2017 to raise money for smaller charities that support veterans across the United States. All money left after expenses from the upcoming performance at the MGM Grand Garden Arena will go to organisations that help military veterans and active-duty service members. Event organisers confirmed that the money will be distributed in partnership with the Combined Arms Institute. Tickets for the concert start at $200, before taxes and other fees. Discounted tickets will also be available specifically for active-duty military personnel and veterans, according to information released by ticket seller AXS. Pre-sales for veterans and active-duty military members will begin on 10 November. Artist pre-sales will follow, while general ticket sales will open to the public on 13 November.Rare onstage appearances for surviving BeatlesAlthough McCartney and Starr have remained close friends and have occasionally worked together in the recording studio, their live performances together have been very rare since The Beatles broke up in 1970. Their most recent public performance together took place in December 2024 at London's O2 Arena. Starr made a surprise appearance during the final night of McCartney's world tour. During the London concert, Starr joined McCartney's touring band on the drums. Together, they performed "Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band" and "Helter Skelter".Before that 2024 appearance, the two musicians had not performed together on stage since 2019. That year, Starr joined McCartney at Dodger Stadium in Los Angeles during an earlier part of his tour. Both musicians have continued performing regularly despite being in their eighties. McCartney completed his long international Got Back tour in late 2024, while Starr has continued touring across North America with his long-running Ringo Starr & His All Starr Band. The upcoming performance in January 2027 at the MGM Grand Garden Arena will give fans one of the few chances this decade to see both surviving members of the famous Liverpool band perform together on stage.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 1962, Neil Armstrong’s X-15 bounced off the atmosphere, overshot Edwards on April 20, then flew over Pasadena: its 12:28 flight became the program’s longest
articles.summary: Discover Neil Armstrong's remarkable 1962 X-15 flight that became a record-breaking adventure. Learn how an unexpected atmospheric bounce led him to overshoot his landing zone near Pasadena and the challenges he faced during this extraordinary test of piloting skills.
articles.body: Neil Armstrong’s most extraordinary flights as a test pilot came in 1962, when he was flying the experimental X-15 rocket plane and encountered something strange as he neared Earth. Moving at approximately one-third the speed of sound, the aircraft passed that target zone at Edwards Air Force Base in California and kept heading out on the course toward Pasadena, ultimately bouncing off the atmosphere. What was intended to be an ordinary test of a new flight control system turned into a surprise test of Armstrong's piloting skills.An experimental aircraft designed to explore the edge of spaceAccording to NASA, the North American X-15 was a joint program with the agency, the US Air Force and the US Navy to investigate the nature of high-speed, high-altitude flight and to develop hypersonic flight vehicle technology, such as vehicle stability and control, and vehicle behaviour during and after hypersonic flight. The X-15 was powered by a rocket engine and lifted into flight from a modified B-52 aircraft flying at an altitude of 45,000 feet. Once at altitude, the rocket engine would be ignited to accelerate the aircraft to hypersonic speed, then shut off, and the aircraft would return to Earth as a glider.The programme was especially significant because traditional aerodynamic controls worked increasingly poorly in the thin air at near-space altitudes. It had reaction control jets, small rocket thrusters that helped pilots move the craft in the thinner atmosphere. Armstrong joined the NASA flight research program in 1955 and was one of the pilots who had tried out the plane. By the spring of 1962, he had already made several X-15 flights and was used to the rigours of sub-orbital high-speed experimental flight.An atmospheric bounce sends Armstrong beyond his intended landing zoneThe 20 April flight test was to determine the performance of the MH-96 adaptive flight control system that was installed in the third X-15 (X-15-3) to help the pilot better control the aerodynamic controls and reaction control thrusters, and to ease the control of the aircraft in varying atmospheric conditions. Armstrong was released from the B-52 mother ship and triggered the X-15 rocket engine. The aircraft climbed to about 207,000 feet (63,000 meters) before the rocket engine burned out.However, it didn't turn out as he had planned. During the pullout, Armstrong pitched the aircraft into a positive angle of attack, causing it to skip back into the upper atmosphere rather than follow the planned flight profile. The unexpected rotation altered the trajectory and left Armstrong significantly farther away from the landing area as the X-15 descended again. Its vehicle was travelling at a speed of around Mach 3 and at an altitude of 100,000 feet. Instead of heading toward Edwards, it continued south until it reached the Pasadena area.NASA recorded the event, stating that the Rose Bowl marked the location where Armstrong was finally able to level off and re-enter the craft back towards the base. The event illustrated the challenges of controlling a plane at high speed as it moved from thin to denser air. A 1965 study of Automatica discusses adaptive flight control design for a re-entry vehicle, with the example of the X-15 control system used as a challenge posed by significant changes in aircraft behaviour at various speeds and altitudes.A difficult return and a record-breaking flightAs noted by NASA, the flight eventually moved towards the Rogers Dry Lake, the actual landing site next to the Edwards Air Force Base. Armstrong landed it on the southern part of Rogers Dry Lake instead of its designated point. The 12-minute, 28.7-second flight was the longest to date and showed how critical pilot judgment was when experimental aircraft encountered conditions that the automatic flight-control system and flight-planning calculations could not foresee. A 2025 study published in Aerospace analysed the flight and suggested a technical explanation using more up-to-date calculations. The researchers reconstructed the flight to examine how aerodynamic instability and the aircraft's finite response time may have contributed to the unexpected path.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 1947, U.S. tea experts tasted imported brews under a 1897 law that set quality standards; the federal tea-tasting system lasted until its repeal in 1996
articles.summary: Explore the unique tradition of U.S. tea tasting, its regulatory history, and the fascinating role of federal experts in ensuring the quality of imported tea from 1947 to 1996.
articles.body: For 99 years, the US had a peculiar tradition: trained tea tasters were in charge of testing imported tea and ensuring it met federal quality standards. Though tasting may sound like a run-of-the-mill exercise, it was in fact part of a regular system, created to ensure that the consumer was getting good quality tea that wasn't adulterated or improperly brewed.A law that brought tea tasting into federal regulationAccording to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, the system dates back to the Tea Importation Act of 1897. Around this time, there was much discussion about the quality and purity of imported tea, especially with respect to adulteration by artificial colouring and foreign substances. To regulate this, Congress enacted a law to establish standards for imported tea and to create a system where the government could designate inspectors to inspect all shipments of imported tea to determine if they conform to the prescribed standards.It was a unique system partly because it depended on human ability to make judgment rather than simply on lab testing. Expert inspectors observed the appearance, aroma, colour, and flavour of the tea after it had been brewed. Using their experience, they could tell the difference between acceptable tea and a beverage that would be rejected by the government. The legislation created a set of guidelines to ensure a consistent approach to imported tea.How federal experts judged imported teaTesting was not just a matter of looking at a cup of tea. Federal examiners compared samples from imported shipments with reference teas that met the minimum standard. The tea standards for different varieties of blended, green, and oolong tea were set by the federal Board of Tea Examiners, which met annually. When they were applied to new shipments, some new criteria were considered, such as the appearance, colour, and flavour of the tea. Defects were looked for, such as stale quality, musty smell, and unnatural colour.If a shipment failed the tests, it could be rejected and returned to the exporting country, or disposed of. The process required familiarity with the nuances of various qualities, since the definition of a well-brewed cup varied by variety and country. Experienced tasters relied on trained olfactory and gustatory senses to pick up subtle differences that might be overlooked on a quick visual inspection. The year 1947 was a notable moment in this history.In 1998, The Washington Post wrote a retrospective piece on the tea industry that recalled how, in 1947, chemist Bob Dick became only the third federal tea examiner. His appointment reflected the specialised nature of the job, which required a detailed understanding of tea quality and consistent examinations. The following year, the Federal Register published the scoring guide issued by the Board of Tea Examiners for the season from 1 May 1948. This was based on Formosa Oolong, China Oolong, Japan Green, and China Gunpowder, showing that the authorities treated varieties separately instead of requiring one global flavour standard for all imported tea.Why the unusual government programme eventually ended However, over the years, the system raised more and more questions about whether there was still any need for a separate federal tea quality program. As part of a wider food safety scheme of the US government, the FDA was empowered to oversee imported food of all kinds, and it also covered tea. By the 1990s, critics suggested the existence of the Board and the separate rules was an expensive and unnecessary layer of bureaucracy. It also struggled for funding and, in the 1996 budget of the FDA, did not include any funding for the Board of Tea Experts, although the industry had helped fund it in the past.Congress eventually passed the Federal Tea Tasters Repeal Act of 1996, signed into law by President Bill Clinton on April 9, 1996. This legislation put an end to the Tea Importation Act of 1897 and the Board of Tea Experts and, in doing so, put an end to the federal system of annual tea quality standards and mandatory taste- testing inspection. The law’s repeal of the federal standards didn't let imported teas off the hook. The FDA still has oversight authority over imports under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act and can now inspect for contamination and consumer safety.You use AI every day. articles.title: A 60-year-old Danish man says ChatGPT told him he could stop paying rent and that losing his home was ‘legally impossible’; after being evicted with his two dogs, he is now suing OpenAI in San Francisco
articles.summary: A 60-year-old Danish man who became homeless after following legal advice generated by ChatGPT has filed a lawsuit against OpenAI in California.
articles.body: A 60-year-old Danish man who became homeless after following legal advice generated by ChatGPT has filed a lawsuit against OpenAI in California. Klaus Elmfelt Aerenlund filed the legal complaint in San Francisco County Superior Court. He claims that ChatGPT told him he could safely stop paying rent during a dispute with his landlord. As a result, he was evicted and forced to live in his car with his two dogs. According to court documents reported by Hoodline and the Daily Journal, the dispute started when Elmfelt's landlord asked him to remove one of his two dogs from his apartment. Looking for advice on how to handle the situation, Elmfelt turned to OpenAI's chatbot. He spent more than 600 hours chatting with the AI models GPT-4o and GPT-5. During these conversations, the chatbot told Elmfelt that he had the legal right to stop paying rent while continuing to live in the apartment.Chatbot assured tenant eviction was impossibleThe lawsuit claims that ChatGPT repeatedly told Elmfelt that Danish rental laws supported his actions. According to details of the lawsuit published by the East Bay Times, the chatbot told Elmfelt that losing his home was "legally impossible." It also claimed that the relevant Danish housing laws were "100% settled" in his favour. To help him deal with the dispute, the chatbot prepared a formal letter for Elmfelt to send to his landlord. In the letter, he officially informed the property owner that he would stop making all future rent payments while the disagreement over his dogs continued. Believing the chatbot's advice, Elmfelt stopped paying rent for three months in a row. However, his landlord began legal proceedings against him. In June 2026, authorities carried out a formal eviction. After losing his home, Elmfelt had nowhere permanent to live. He spent several weeks sleeping in his car with his two dogs. He later found temporary accommodation in a small cabin at a local campsite, according to the lawsuit.Parasocial bond and financial fantasiesThe court documents also describe how Elmfelt became deeply dependent on the AI system. According to the complaint, the chatbot gradually took on the roles of a personal friend, legal adviser, and business partner. As reported by Hoodline, the chatbot regularly agreed with Elmfelt's questions and concerns with complete confidence, even when its answers were wrong. When he began to question the information, the chatbot reportedly told him that he was not delusional but was simply "ahead of the curve." The lawsuit also explains how the software encouraged him to develop unrealistic expectations about his finances. According to the complaint, ChatGPT told Elmfelt that an internal sales team was actively working to sell his products. It also claimed that the team was building a business worth billions of dollars. During these conversations, the chatbot created detailed personal budgets for international holidays, expensive household appliances, and luxury homes in New York City.Plaintiff demands safeguards and damagesElmfelt is seeking an unspecified amount of money from OpenAI to cover the losses and suffering he says were caused by his eviction. He cites serious emotional distress, financial problems, worsening depression, and social isolation. Along with financial compensation, the lawsuit asks the court to order OpenAI to change how its AI software communicates with users. According to the legal complaint, Elmfelt wants the court to require OpenAI to introduce technical safeguards. These measures would aim to stop its AI models from giving false legal advice or encouraging users who express delusional or unrealistic beliefs about themselves. The lawsuit is one of the first cases in the United States in which a person has directly blamed AI-generated advice for their eviction and the homelessness that followed. OpenAI has not publicly responded to requests for comment about the lawsuit filed in San Francisco.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: End Iran war or tackle Trump? What Americans want Democrat-held Congress to focus on
articles.summary: As US President Donald Trump's war with Iran drags on with little sign of progress, majorities of Americans want the newly elected Democratic-majority
articles.body: As US President Donald Trump's war with Iran drags on with little sign of progress, majorities of Americans want the newly elected Democratic-majority Congress to step in to end the conflict and repeal tariffs imposed by the MAGA chief.The demand comes days after Republicans lost control of Congress in the midterm elections, with voters increasingly focused on the rising cost of living.A new Reuters/Ipsos poll found that 71% of Americans support legislation to end the US conflict with Iran, while 62% favour repealing tariffs imposed by President Trump.The findings point to strong public demand for the incoming Democratic-majority Congress to act on two issues that have weighed on household budgets.The four-day poll, conducted online across the US and completed on Monday, found that support for ending the war crossed party lines.As many as 93% of Democrats and 51% of Republicans backed legislation to end the conflict, which the US launched alongside ally Israel in February.Democrats secured majorities in both the House of Representatives and the Senate in last week's midterm elections, dealing a setback to Trump's Republicans. The new Congress is scheduled to take office on January 3.Cost of living tops Americans' agendaThe war with Iran has pushed fuel prices higher, adding to inflationary pressures from tariffs imposed on hundreds of imported goods.Trump has defended the military campaign as necessary to prevent Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon. He has argued that tariffs will protect American industry from cheaper imports.Democratic leaders have pledged to focus on the cost of living and have said they will seek to force an end to the war. Many have also promised to challenge Trump's tariffs.The poll found that nine in 10 Americans want Congress to prioritise cost-of-living issues during its first 100 days. Fewer respondents wanted lawmakers to focus on issues such as artificial intelligence regulation, immigration reform and climate change.Despite the sharp political divide, large majorities across both parties said Trump should make an effort to work with Democrats and that Democratic leaders in Congress should also try to work with the president.Americans divided over possible impeachmentWhile voters want the new Congress to act on the war and tariffs, they appear less united on how far Democrats should go in confronting Trump.Some 42% of respondents said it would be “bad for the country” if the new Congress tried to impeach the president, while 33% said such a move would be good for the country.The remaining respondents were unsure or did not answer. Democrats themselves remain divided over how to reduce healthcare costs and how aggressively to pursue Trump, including whether to seek his impeachment or that of members of his cabinet.Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth is expected to face a House impeachment vote this week after a Republican lawmaker initiated the move.Trump said after the elections that he would “probably” get along with Democrats. However, he also promoted Stephen Miller, a polarising aide who has called the Democratic Party a domestic extremist group, to the position of White House chief of staff.Trump's approval rating remains near career lowAccording to a Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted online across the US from November 6 to 9, 32% of Americans approved of Trump's performance as president.The figure was unchanged from two previous Reuters/Ipsos polls conducted between late October and early November, and one percentage point above his career-low rating of 31% recorded in mid-October.The survey also suggested that Democrats have yet to translate their electoral gains into broad public popularity. Some 45% of Americans viewed the Democratic Party favourably, while 51% had an unfavourable opinion. For Republicans, the corresponding figures were 35% and 60%.The Reuters/Ipsos poll surveyed 1,705 US adults nationwide between November 6 and 9. It had a margin of error of approximately two percentage points.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Trump puts his chips on Huang as China spy storm gathers force
articles.summary: TOI correspondent in Washington: In Washington, national security issues usually require a healthy dose of suspicion, particularly where China is
articles.body: TOI correspondent in Washington: In Washington, national security issues usually require a healthy dose of suspicion, particularly where China is concerned. But in a remarkable display of trust, US President Donald Trump is repeatedly vouching for Nvidia chief Jensen Huang following disclosures that he may have been ensnared in a Chinese honey-trap.Speaking at the White House on Monday after revealing he had spoken to Huang, Trump described him as “a great, brilliant person, and we want to protect our brilliant people." Asked whether Huang knew that the woman he was having an affair with was allegedly a Chinese intelligence operative, Trump recounted asking him directly. " He said, 'I had no idea that she was a spy.' And I really believe him." He also said Huang was "suffering greatly," particularly because of the effect on his family.On the FBI investigation, Trump offered reassurance rather than alarm: "I know the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he'll be in good shape." He even appeared reluctant to contemplate losing Huang as a presidential adviser or off-loading him on an upcoming trip to Asia, saying he would like the Nvidia boss to remain in his role and he had always found him "very above board.”It was an extraordinary display of presidential confidence in a man whose company is being investigated by both spooks and lawmakers, coming as it did at a politically vulnerable time when Trump has received a drubbing in the mid-term elections. Lawmakers are champing at the bit to investigate an administration they accuse of excessive coziness with powerful technology billionaires, and the Huang affair offers an unusually convenient intersection of national security, corporate influence, China policy -- and Trump’s own financial interests.The president’s critics are now zeroing in on his financial disclosures in filings before the Office of Government Ethics that show Trump investment accounts bought between $500,001 and $1 million of Nvidia shares on January 6, 2026, and between $1 million and $5 million on February 10. A September filing disclosed that the account bought as much as $1.6 million and sold as much as $1 million in Nvidia stock during August alone.These are not necessarily straightforward purchases made personally by Trump. The filings cover transactions in accounts associated with the president and his family, and the White House has repeatedly explained that independent third-party financial institutions manage the portfolio, replicating recognised indexes, including the Schwab 1000, and investment decisions are made without presidential input.But given reports of widespread grift and corruption by Trump loyalists, lawmakers are raring to investigate the matter under overarching concerns about China -- not that Congress, including Democratic lawmakers, are strangers to charges of insider trading. Democratic Senator Chris Coons, who will become chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, has said he wants an investigation into the relationship between the Trump administration, foreign intelligence operatives and AI billionaires, pointing to a broader probe that could soon sweep up tech tycoons."I'm not interested in investigating people just because I don't like them. I want to investigate them because I suspect they've put our national security at risk, they've been breaking the law and lying to the American people," Coons said amid growing fears that the Huang affair would prick the AI bubble on which much of the U.S stock market currently rests.Tech analysts meanwhile are digging into Huang’s long and well-chronicled battle to sell advanced chips to China despite deep suspicion in Washington that it could result in the US ceding its lead in artificial intelligence. In an April 2026 interview to tech podcaster Dwarkesh Patel that is now being viewed with renewed interest, Huang repeatedly bats for selling advanced chips to China.Dwarkesh: Why would we want to sell China the materials for a serious cyberweapon? articles.title: An Ohio landowner admitted filling holes near a farm drain with shoes, rocks and license plates, then sued his neighbour over runoff; a 2026 appeals court upheld $126,198 in legal fees and expenses against him
articles.summary: An Ohio landowner who admitted putting shoes, rocks, and number plates into holes near a farm drainage pipe before suing his neighbour over water runoff
articles.body: An Ohio landowner who admitted putting shoes, rocks, and number plates into holes near a farm drainage pipe before suing his neighbour over water runoff has been ordered to pay more than $126,000 in legal fees and expenses. An appeals court has upheld the penalty against him. The decision by the Fifth District Court of Appeals of Ohio confirmed an earlier ruling that James Helfrich had engaged in frivolous conduct during his long-running legal dispute with his neighbours, Foor Family Investments, LLC.The appeals court decision, filed under case number 2026 CA 00024 in the Licking County Court of Common Pleas, is the latest development in a legal battle that lasted several years. The dispute involved farm drainage pipes and damage to neighbouring properties. According to court documents published on Justia Law, Helfrich originally sued his neighbours, claiming that water running off their land had damaged his farm. However, during court testimony under oath, Helfrich admitted that he had personally filled holes above the underground drainage system with household rubbish and scrap materials. Instead of repairing the damaged pipe or contacting his neighbours, he chose to block the holes himself."When they asked what I put in there, I said, 'I don't care what it was. I filled the hole with shoes, with rocks, license plates, anything. It didn't matter to me what I put down there,'" Helfrich said during the trial, according to official court transcripts cited in the appeals court opinion.Self-help repairs lead to legal counterclaimHelfrich told the court that he had put the rubbish into the holes to protect his family, friends, and livestock from falling into dangerous openings in the field. He also admitted that he could have repaired the damaged drainage pipe that caused the holes or asked his neighbour, Ron Foor, to arrange the repairs. However, he chose not to do either. After Helfrich filed his lawsuit, Foor Family Investments submitted a formal response and filed a counterclaim. The company asked the court for financial compensation and a legal drainage easement across the property. During a jury trial in Licking County in August 2021, Helfrich represented himself in his own claims. However, a lawyer provided by his insurance company represented him against the counterclaim.The jury ruled against Helfrich, rejecting his claims and ordering him to pay Foor Family Investments $30,000 (£23,000) in damages. The jury also established an easement by estoppel over the property. This decision was later upheld by an appeals court in 2022. After the first verdict, Foor Family Investments filed additional requests asking the court to award interest on the damages, legal fees, and court costs. The company argued that Helfrich had engaged in frivolous legal conduct because he continued with claims that had no proper basis, despite knowing that he had blocked the drainage system himself.Appeals court confirms sanctions for frivolous litigationAfter further court proceedings, the trial court agreed with the neighbouring landowners. It found that Helfrich's legal actions met Ohio's legal definition of frivolous conduct. The court ordered him to pay $126,198 (£97,000) to cover the legal fees and other expenses Foor Family Investments had faced during the dispute. Helfrich challenged the financial penalty at the Fifth District Court of Appeals. He raised several arguments, claiming that the trial judge had used his authority incorrectly, mishandled requests for a new trial, and wrongly decided that his legal actions were frivolous.Writing for the three-judge appeals court panel, Judge Robert G. Montgomery upheld the lower court's decision in full. Judges William B. Hoffman and Craig R. Baldwin joined him in the ruling. The appeals court explained that Ohio law, including the Ohio Revised Code and Civil Rule 11, gives judges wide powers to impose financial penalties when someone files legal documents without proper legal grounds or mainly to delay proceedings and create unnecessary costs."When evaluating a motion for sanctions, a court must assess whether the person signing the document has read the pleading, harbors good grounds to support it to the best of his or her knowledge, information, and belief, and did not file it for purposes of delay," the court explained in its written opinion.The three judges concluded that the trial court had acted within its legal powers when reviewing the evidence and ordering Helfrich to pay $126,198. The payment is intended to cover the legal expenses his neighbour faced while defending against the claims over several years.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Unesco: Women ahead in higher edu, but rural-urban gap hits schoolgirls
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: India has made substantial progress in closing the gender gap in education, with women now outpacing men in higher education.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India has made substantial progress in closing the gender gap in education, with women now outpacing men in higher education. But a rural-urban divide continues to disadvantage girls at the school-completion stage. A Unesco report found that for every 100 boys completing upper secondary education in rural India, only 59 girls do so, compared with gender parity in urban areas. India has closed at least 65% of its initial disparity in upper secondary completion since 2000.The 2026 Global Education Monitoring report, Gender Equity in Access to Education, puts India's overall gender parity index for upper secondary completion at 0.89, or 89 girls for every 100 boys. In rural areas, it falls to 0.59.Unesco categorises India as having made "fast progress" among countries with large disadvantages for girls at the start of the century. This applies to students completing school within the expected age window and those finishing late.Recent govt data point to improvements in participation and retention. UDISE+ 2025-26 shows girls account for 48.4% of school enrolment. The secondary-stage dropout rate fell from 8.2% in 2024-25 to 7%, while retention rose from 47.2% to 51.9%. These indicators cannot be directly compared with Unesco's household-survey-based completion ratios.At college level, women lead men. AISHE 2023-24 puts the female gross enrolment ratio at 31.2%, against 28.9% for males. Women's enrolment rose from 1.57 crore in 2014-15 to 2.24 crore, a 42.2% increase. The higher education gender parity index stood at 1.08, with women's participation exceeding men's for seven consecutive years.Unesco's review of Indian studies found free school lunches had nearly twice the impact on primary enrolment for girls as for boys in disadvantaged rural communities. Separate toilets helped raise enrolment among adolescent girls, while girls' clubs offering life skills and social support modestly improved secondary completion in Karnataka.Globally, Unesco found parity in enrolment from pre-primary through upper secondary school. Women increasingly outnumber men in higher education, with 88 male students for every 100 women enrolled and 82 male graduates. Yet 273 million children and young people were out of education in 2024.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: A man dressed as Batman chased a suspected handbag thief through Norwich, then scaled a high cathedral wall to retrieve the abandoned bag and return it with every item intact
articles.summary: A man dressed as Batman chased a suspected handbag thief through Norwich after witnessing a woman’s bag being snatched outside a nightclub.
articles.body: A man dressed as Batman chased a suspected handbag thief through Norwich after witnessing a woman’s bag being snatched outside a nightclub. Sonni Mason, 25, was attending a fancy-dress party when he joined the pursuit alongside people dressed as Poison Ivy and Mister Fantastic. Although the group caught up with the suspected thief, the handbag was missing. Following a tip-off, they discovered it approximately 300 metres away, on top of a high flint wall surrounding Norwich Cathedral. Mason then climbed the wall, still wearing his Batman costume, retrieved the bag and returned it to its owner with all its contents intact.How did Batman chase the suspected handbag thief in NorwichAccording to the Guardian, Mason and the other costumed partygoers pursued the suspected thief and alerted a group of police officers who were on their way. However, when they caught up with the suspect, he no longer had the handbag. The group subsequently received a tip-off about where the missing property had been left.The handbag was eventually discovered approximately 300 metres from the location where it had been snatched. It had been left on top of a high flint wall along the perimeter of Norwich Cathedral. The group initially attempted to retrieve it using a roll of toilet paper, but their efforts were unsuccessful.How did Batman retrieve the stolen handbagWith the handbag still out of reach, Mason decided to climb the wall himself. Still wearing his full Batman costume, he scaled the high structure and managed to retrieve the bag. He then returned it to its owner, with all the contents still inside.Much of the incident was captured in a TikTok video uploaded to Mason's account. In a post accompanying the footage, he described how the group had become involved in the incident while celebrating a friend's birthday."On a night out for a friend's birthday, someone swiped someone's bag over a pack of cigarettes out of spite… myself as Batman, Poison Ivy, Mr Fantastic and various other heroes chased him down," Mason wrote.What did Mason say about helping others like BatmanSpeaking to the SWNS news agency, Mason, who is from London and works in a cafe, said he hoped the incident would encourage people to help others when they witnessed someone in trouble."I hope I can inspire people to be a little bit more like Batman. Not so much the running around in the dark in a costume but helping others out. I didn’t expect to be scaling up a wall," he said.He also explained that helping people did not require wearing a superhero costume. "Everyone needs a little bit of Batman. You have to be brave, bold and kind. I would hope everyone else would do the same, whether or not they are wearing a cape or a cowl," Mason added.Mason said his intention was not to imitate the superhero's physical fights or rooftop pursuits, but to make sure everyone was safe. Referring to Batman's role as a protector, he said: "That’s what [Batman] is about. He’s a protector."He further expressed hope that people would be encouraged to intervene appropriately when they saw someone being mugged or made to feel uncomfortable during a night out, adding that "it shouldn’t take a superhero costume to make you want to do that."What did Norfolk Police confirm about the missing handbagNorfolk Police confirmed that officers had been approached about the missing handbag during routine night-time patrols in Norwich on Saturday, September 19.A police spokesperson said: "Officers on routine night-time economy patrols in Norwich were approached by a member of the public, on Saturday, September 19, who requested help to find a missing bag."The spokesperson confirmed that the handbag was subsequently located and returned to its owner. "Following inquiries at the scene, the bag was located with all of its contents intact and subsequently returned to its owner," the statement added.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient.
